title: Double moss stitch baby blanket
subtitle: A 75 by 90 cm cot blanket in DK double moss stitch.
excerpt: A 75 by 90 cm cot blanket worked flat in double moss stitch (UK: double moss; US: seed stitch) on 4 mm needles. Double moss groups the knit and purl stitches in pairs over a four-row repeat, producing a larger block texture than single seed stitch. About 260 g of DK.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, 5th series (1889), §Knitted Toilet Covers, describes double moss stitch as a standard flat-lying textured fabric for nursery items. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), §Moss Stitch Variations, explains double moss as a four-row extension of seed stitch and notes its use for afghans and baby blankets.

glossaryTerms.term: Double moss stitch (US: seed stitch variant)
glossaryTerms.definition: A four-row stitch repeat that groups knit and purl stitches in pairs. Rows 1 and 2: *k2, p2; repeat. Rows 3 and 4: *p2, k2; repeat. The knit and purl blocks alternate in a checkerboard over the four rows, producing a larger pebbly texture than single seed stitch. Lies flat without blocking.

content.text: A single-panel rectangle worked flat in
double moss stitch
on 4 mm needles, finishing at 75 cm wide by 90 cm long.

A single panel requires no seaming. Double moss stitch was chosen for its texture: the four-row repeat groups the knit and purl stitches in pairs, producing a bolder surface than single seed stitch without requiring any new technique beyond knit and purl. Like garter and single seed stitch, double moss lies flat on both faces without blocking, which makes it practical for a baby blanket. Budget about 260 g (about 570 m / 625 yards) of machine-washable DK. Buy all the yarn at once in matched dye lots. Drapes across a cot or folds for a pram bag.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: 260 g (about 570 m / 625 yards) of DK-weight machine-washable yarn

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) circular needle, 80 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

22 stitches and 38 rows to 10 cm over double moss stitch on 4 mm needles, unblocked. Double moss sits slightly shorter per row than plain garter. Swatch the full 4-row repeat for at least 15 cm before casting on.
If your row gauge is 36 rows per 10 cm instead of 38, the blanket will be about 94 cm long at 342 rows rather than 90 cm. Measure by tape, not by row count.
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast-on
Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 164 stitches (a multiple of 4 for the stitch repeat). Long-tail tail: (4 × 164) / 10 + 15 = 65.6 + 15 = 81 cm. Measure 90 cm of tail.
Body
Row 1 (RS): *k2, p2; repeat from * to end.
Row 2 (WS): *k2, p2; repeat from * to end.
Row 3 (RS): *p2, k2; repeat from * to end.
Row 4 (WS): *p2, k2; repeat from * to end.
Repeat rows 1 to 4 until the blanket measures 90 cm from the cast-on edge. The four-row repeat is easy to track: rows 1 and 2 start k2; rows 3 and 4 start p2.
When you set this aside between sessions, note which of the four rows you are on. Jot it as "1", "2", "3", or "4" on a sticky note.
Stitch count check-ins

At row 171 (about 45 cm, end of a complete repeat): count across. You should have 164 stitches (a multiple of 4). At row 340 (about 89.5 cm): count again. If the count is correct and a multiple of 4, cast off on the next row.
Common faults

Pattern developing diagonal stripes: rows 1 and 2 were worked correctly but rows 3 and 4 were accidentally worked as rows 1 and 2 again, shifting the pattern offset. Keep a row number tally if the four-row position is hard to read from the fabric.

Loose purl stitches visible as wider bumps in the checkerboard: purl tension looser than knit tension. Work each purl stitch firmly, or try a needle one size smaller until the purl tension tightens to match the knit tension.
Cast-off
Cast off in pattern (k the knits, p the purls) with a relaxed tension. End on row 2 or row 4 of the repeat if possible so the top and bottom edges match.
Finishing
Weave in both ends on the wrong side, running each tail at least 5 cm along a row of double moss stitch and changing direction once. Trim.
Care
Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle if superwash DK. Lay flat to dry. The double moss texture relaxes and the purl squares become more even after a wash and flat dry.
What to try next

From double moss stitch, the natural progression is basket weave stitch: a longer repeat (typically six or eight stitches) that produces raised rectangular blocks. Basket weave and double moss use the same knit-and-purl technique and the same 4 mm needle; only the block size changes.
